bands.name: Runs itself
bands.summary: This one takes care of itself. Spend your attention elsewhere.

bands.name: Lightly guided
bands.summary: Comfortable. A light hand keeps it exactly where it is.

bands.name: Responds well
bands.summary: Ordinary machinery that gives back roughly what you put in.

bands.name: Rewards attention
bands.summary: Give this one real effort and you will feel the difference.

bands.name: Your biggest lever
bands.summary: The highest-return system you own. Small consistent changes move this a long way.

markers.impact: The fast-twitch structural protein — and how muscle copes with hard eccentric work

CC: Both copies of alpha-actinin-3 present. Fast, forceful contraction comes naturally — and so does more muscle damage from downhill running and heavy eccentric sets. Your recovery days are load-bearing, not optional.
CT: One working copy. You sit in the most common and most flexible place: sprint work and long steady work both land well. Train whichever you enjoy.
TT: No alpha-actinin-3, like roughly one in five people worldwide. Muscle leans oxidative — you take less damage from eccentric work and recover from it faster. Power is still fully trainable; it just builds rather than arrives.

markers.impact: Recycles energy inside working muscle when demand outruns supply

CC: Full AMP deaminase activity. Your muscle recycles its own energy currency efficiently during hard efforts — one of the cleanest results in this panel.
CT: One reduced copy. Most people notice nothing; a few find late-session heavy work feels heavier than the pace suggests. Carbohydrate around the session covers it.
TT: Both copies reduced. Cramping and stiff, sore muscles after big sessions are common, and creatine kinase can read high without meaning overtraining. Worth telling any clinician who orders a CK — this is the single most misread result in athlete bloods.

markers.impact: Switches on fat burning for long efforts

GG: The common setting. Fat oxidation comes online readily on long steady work, which spares glycogen for when you actually need it.
CG: Mixed. Fat burning is available but slightly slower to arrive — a proper 15-minute warm-up genuinely earns its place for you.
CC: Leans on carbohydrate earlier. Long sessions go much better with fuel taken on board rather than trained through. This is a practical eating decision, not a limit.

markers.impact: Builds oxidative muscle fibre and moves fat into the furnace

CC: Strong fat-handling setting. Your metabolic flexibility — switching from glycogen to fat mid-effort — is one of your advantages.
CT: Middle ground. Flexibility improves noticeably with steady-state aerobic volume.
TT: Carbohydrate is your preferred fuel. Perfectly fine — it means fuelling strategy matters more to you than to most on efforts over ninety minutes.

markers.impact: The master switch for building new mitochondria

GG: The strongest mitochondrial-building setting. Aerobic base work pays you back quickly.
AG: Typical. Mitochondrial adaptation arrives on the ordinary schedule — six to eight weeks of consistent aerobic work.
AA: Mitochondrial density builds more gradually. Consistency beats intensity for you: frequent easy aerobic work outperforms sporadic hard sessions.

markers.impact: Sets how much fuel becomes work and how much becomes heat

GG: Tight energy coupling — efficient conversion of fuel into work.
AG: Balanced. A little more energy released as heat, which is why you may run warm in sessions.
AA: More uncoupled. You lose slightly more energy as heat and generate fewer free radicals doing it — a genuine trade, not a shortfall.

markers.impact: Thyroid signalling into resting metabolic rate and lean mass

CC: The common setting; associated in some cohorts with slightly higher lean mass. Evidence is thin — carried here for completeness, not for action.
CT: No practical difference established. Reported so you can see the whole panel.
TT: No practical difference established. Reported so you can see the whole panel.

markers.impact: Rapid energy regeneration for explosive efforts — and a common source of misread bloods

TT: Strong creatine-kinase system. Repeat sprints and heavy singles are well supported.
CT: Typical phosphocreatine turnover. Nothing follows from this result on its own — it is one input into the whole-report synthesis, not a recommendation.
CC: Slightly slower phosphocreatine turnover. Longer rests between heavy sets do more for you than they do for most people.

markers.impact: Muscle growth signalling in response to resistance training

AA: Associated with a strong hypertrophy response to resistance work in small studies. Evidence is early — treat as interest, not instruction.
AC: Middle. No practical change to how you should train.
CC: No practical change to how you should train. Reported for completeness.

markers.impact: Fat storage, insulin sensitivity and how you respond to dietary fat

CC: The common setting. Your insulin sensitivity tracks closely with body composition, sleep and how much you move on ordinary days — real leverage here.
CG: Carries Ala12, associated with better insulin sensitivity. One of the best-evidenced metabolic markers in this panel.
GG: Two copies of Ala12. Favourable insulin handling; unusually well replicated for a single SNP.

markers.impact: Makes nitric oxide — the signal that opens blood vessels during effort

GG: Full nitric-oxide production. Vessels open readily under load and oxygen gets where it is needed.
GT: Slightly reduced output. Dietary nitrate — beetroot, rocket, spinach — has a measurably larger effect in people carrying this than in those who do not.
TT: Lower nitric-oxide output. This is a food answer with real evidence behind it: nitrate-rich leafy greens most days, and a proper warm-up so vessels are open before the hard part starts.

markers.impact: Blood-pressure and fluid regulation during exercise (the classic I/D marker)

GG: Leans toward the insertion pattern — associated with muscle efficiency and endurance in several athlete cohorts.
CG: Mixed. In practice this is the most versatile setting: both endurance and power work suit you.
CC: Leans toward the deletion pattern — associated with power output, and with a firmer blood-pressure response to heavy effort. Sodium balance and a real cool-down matter more for you.

markers.impact: Angiotensinogen — upstream of blood-pressure control

AA: The lower-activity setting. Blood pressure under load tends to look after itself.
AG: Intermediate. Your blood-pressure response is genuinely salt-responsive — meaning the amount you add is one of the few dietary changes that shows up in a measurement.
GG: Higher angiotensinogen. Balance sodium against what you actually lose in sweat rather than cutting it blindly, and get blood pressure checked at rest yearly. High leverage, simple actions.

markers.impact: Bradykinin signalling — vessel widening and muscle efficiency

CC: Standard receptor expression. Blood flow to muscle behaves conventionally.
CT: Higher receptor expression, associated with better mechanical efficiency in endurance work — you do more with the same oxygen.
TT: Highest receptor expression. Efficient blood flow into working muscle; pairs well with the nitric-oxide result above.

markers.impact: Grows new capillaries into trained muscle

GG: Strong capillary-building signal. Base aerobic work translates into real vascular change for you.
CG: Typical. Capillary density builds on the usual timeline with consistent aerobic volume.
CC: Slower to build new capillaries. Longer, easier aerobic sessions do more for you here than short hard ones.

markers.impact: Adrenaline's main receptor — airway opening, blood flow and fat release

GG: Receptors respond strongly to adrenaline but also desensitise faster with repeated stimulation. Practically: your body answers hard efforts quickly, and back-to-back high days blunt that answer.
AG: The balanced setting — responsive without desensitising quickly.
AA: Receptors hold their sensitivity but respond more modestly. Warm-ups matter; the response builds rather than switches on.

markers.impact: The second adrenaline-receptor variant — vessel tone and fat mobilisation

CC: Standard. Fat release under adrenaline behaves conventionally.
CG: Mixed and well protected against receptor down-regulation. A comfortable place to sit.
GG: Resistant to desensitisation — the adrenaline response holds up across a long block of hard training.

markers.impact: Iron absorption — the single most important safety marker in this panel

GG: No C282Y variant. Iron is handled normally and iron questions are ordinary ones.
AG: One copy of C282Y. You absorb iron more readily than most. Never take iron without a ferritin and transferrin saturation first — athletes are handed iron for fatigue constantly, and for you that is the wrong default.
AA: Two copies of C282Y. This warrants a proper haemochromatosis assessment with your doctor — iron studies, and a family conversation. Iron supplements are blocked in SAM for you regardless of what any fatigue score says.

markers.impact: The second iron-absorption variant (H63D)

CC: No H63D variant.
CG: One copy. Mild effect on iron absorption on its own. Worth knowing before anyone hands you an iron tablet — check ferritin first.
GG: Two copies. Mild on its own, more relevant alongside C282Y. Iron studies before iron supplements, always.

markers.impact: Sets hepcidin — the hormone that decides how much dietary iron you actually keep

AA: Higher hepcidin, so you keep less of the iron you eat. Combine iron-rich food with vitamin C, keep it away from coffee and tea, and have ferritin checked yearly if you train hard. Food-first, and genuinely effective.
AG: Intermediate. Timing matters more than amount — iron-rich meals away from tea and coffee.
GG: Efficient iron retention from ordinary food.

markers.impact: Baseline level of the body's main inflammation signal

CC: Higher baseline C-reactive protein. This is one of the most lifestyle-responsive numbers in medicine — sleep, aerobic volume, oily fish and body composition all move it measurably. Ask for hs-CRP at your next draw, and never within 72 hours of a hard session.
CT: Intermediate baseline. Same advice, lower stakes: measure it rested, not after training.
TT: Lower baseline inflammatory signal. A quiet system that recovers cleanly.

markers.impact: The signal muscle releases during exercise — repair when brief, drag when prolonged

GG: Higher IL-6 response to hard work. You feel big sessions for longer than training partners do. Two days between maximal sessions is not conservative for you — it is the correct spacing.
CG: Intermediate response. Ordinary recovery timelines apply.
CC: Lower IL-6 response. Muscle repair after eccentric work is efficient and you turn sessions around quickly.

markers.impact: How strongly cells hear the IL-6 signal

AA: Standard receptor signalling.
AC: Intermediate. More of the receptor circulates in soluble form, which shifts inflammatory signalling slightly.
CC: More soluble receptor. Associated with a modestly different inflammatory profile — no action, reported for completeness.

markers.impact: Tumour necrosis factor — the fast, loud end of inflammatory signalling

GG: The common, lower-output setting. Inflammation starts and stops cleanly.
AG: Higher TNF output. Inflammatory responses run hot and long — after training, after illness, after a short night. Sleep is your most powerful anti-inflammatory and it is not a metaphor.
AA: Highest TNF output. Prioritise sleep duration and spacing between maximal sessions above every supplement in existence. Worth asking for hs-CRP and IL-6 rested at your next draw.

markers.impact: The mitochondria's own antioxidant — first line against exercise free radicals

GG: The efficient import setting — the enzyme reaches the mitochondria where it is needed.
AG: Intermediate. Colourful plants across the week do the work here; high-dose antioxidant capsules around training can blunt the adaptation you trained for.
AA: Less enzyme reaches the mitochondria. Real leverage, and food-shaped: berries, brassicas, olive oil, herbs, green tea. Not megadose vitamin C and E around sessions — that is the one intervention shown to reduce training adaptation.

markers.impact: The antioxidant that works outside cells, in blood and tissue fluid

CC: Standard extracellular antioxidant defence, well distributed in tissue.
CG: Carrier. More enzyme circulates and less stays bound in tissue — a distribution difference rather than a shortfall.
GG: Rare. Same distribution difference, more pronounced. No action established.

markers.impact: Attaches glutathione to reactive compounds so they can leave

AA: Full enzyme activity. Reactive by-products of hard training are conjugated and cleared efficiently.
AG: Reduced activity in one copy. Sulphur-rich vegetables — broccoli, rocket, garlic, onions — feed this pathway directly.
GG: Lowest activity of the three. Cruciferous vegetables most days, and limit what you ask the pathway to clear: smoke, excess alcohol, and unnecessary painkillers. Cheap, food-first, high return.

markers.impact: An entire glutathione enzyme that some people are simply born without

PRESENT: Present. This clearance route is available to you.
HET: One copy. Capacity is reduced but the route is open — sulphur-rich vegetables keep it well fed.
NULL: Absent — as it is in roughly a fifth of people. You rely more on the other glutathione routes, which makes them worth feeding daily: brassicas, alliums, eggs, protein. Nothing about this is a flaw; it is one of the commonest human variations there is.

markers.assayNote: Copy-number, not a SNP — the lab reports present or absent, not a genotype. Confirm the array design calls the deletion rather than tagging it.

markers.impact: A second glutathione clearance route, also commonly absent

AA: Full activity on this route.
AG: Intermediate activity. Well supported by ordinary sulphur-rich food.
GG: Reduced activity. Leans your clearance onto the other glutathione enzymes — worth feeding them properly.

markers.impact: Clears the products of fat oxidation inside cell membranes

GG: Higher expression. Membrane lipid by-products from long sessions are cleared efficiently.
AG: Intermediate expression. Olive oil, nuts and oily fish support membrane repair directly.
AA: Lower expression. Long endurance blocks generate more of exactly what this enzyme handles — food-based antioxidants across the day beat a capsule around the session.

markers.impact: Diamine oxidase — clears histamine from food, in the gut, before it reaches your circulation

CC: Full diamine oxidase activity. Aged cheese, wine, cured meat and leftovers are handled without event.
CG: Reduced activity. You will likely notice a pattern — flushing, a blocked nose or a headache after aged, fermented or reheated food, especially after a hard aerobic session when histamine is already up.
GG: Low diamine oxidase activity. This is your single most actionable food result. Freshness is the whole intervention: cook and eat, rather than cook and keep. Track it for two weeks before you change anything permanently — the pattern is usually obvious.

markers.impact: Clears histamine inside tissue — brain, lungs, skin — after it has done its job

AA: The slower-clearing setting on the direction currently selected. Combined with exercise, which raises histamine on its own, this is why hard aerobic weeks can come with a blocked nose, itchy skin and restless sleep. Airway, bedroom air and fresh food are the levers.
AG: Intermediate tissue clearance. Usually only noticeable during high aerobic volume or high pollen weeks.
GG: Faster tissue clearance. Histamine is cleared promptly once it has done its work.

markers.impact: The main structural collagen in tendon, ligament and bone

GG: The common setting. Collagen strength tracks your training history and protein intake rather than your genotype.
GT: Associated with favourable collagen ratios and, in several cohorts, fewer ligament injuries.
TT: Associated with the most favourable collagen ratio of the three. Still train the tissue — tendon adapts to slow heavy load, not to luck.

markers.impact: Regulates how tightly collagen fibrils pack — tendon stiffness and range

TT: The stiffer-tendon setting. Associated with less flexibility and, in several studies, more Achilles trouble. Slow heavy calf and hamstring loading twice a week is the intervention with actual evidence behind it — not stretching.
CT: Intermediate. Ordinary tendon conditioning suits you.
CC: The more compliant setting. Greater range, and a little more demand on the muscle to control it — strength through full range is your protection.

markers.impact: Organises how collagen fibrils bind into ligament

AA: The common setting for fibril organisation.
AG: Intermediate. Nothing to change; contributes a small amount to the connective-tissue picture below.
GG: Associated in some ACL cohorts with different ligament organisation. Small effect, reported in the composite rather than acted on alone.

markers.impact: Breaks down old matrix so new tissue can be laid in — the remodelling side of repair

AA: Standard remodelling rate.
AG: Intermediate remodelling. Progress load in steps rather than jumps and the tissue keeps up.
GG: Different remodelling rate; studied mostly in Achilles injury with mixed results. Feeds the composite, not a standalone finding.

markers.impact: Collagen breakdown rate in the promoter of the main collagenase

1G/1G: Lower collagenase expression — slower matrix turnover.
2G/2G: Higher collagenase expression. Contributes to the connective-tissue composite below.

markers.assayNote: A promoter insertion/deletion (1G/2G), not a SNP. Confirm the array calls the indel directly rather than tagging it.

markers.impact: Builds and maintains cartilage, tendon and ligament at the joint

CC: Higher GDF5 expression — good cartilage maintenance signalling.
CT: Intermediate expression. Strength around the joint is what protects cartilage; this is where it pays.
TT: Lower expression of a growth factor that maintains cartilage. Practically: build and keep muscle around your knees and hips, keep body weight steady, and treat joint niggles early rather than training through them. Genuinely high leverage over a career.

markers.impact: The natural brake on interleukin-1 inside a joint

TT: Strong natural braking on joint inflammation.
CT: Intermediate braking. Ordinary joint care applies.
CC: Less braking on joint inflammation. Oily fish, sleep and sensible load progression are the practical levers.

markers.impact: Immune regulation during tissue repair

AA: Standard immune regulation through repair.
AG: Intermediate. No action established.
GG: Associated with different autoimmune-related regulation in population studies. Not an athletic finding; reported for completeness.

markers.impact: Vitamin D receptor (BsmI) — how strongly bone hears vitamin D

GG: Associated with higher bone mineral density in several populations.
AG: Intermediate. Vitamin D status and weight-bearing work both matter on the usual schedule.
AA: Associated with lower bone density. This is a strong argument for measuring 25-OH vitamin D rather than guessing, and for keeping impact and resistance work in your week for life.

markers.impact: Vitamin D receptor (FokI) — the length, and efficiency, of the receptor protein

GG: The shorter, more active receptor. Efficient vitamin D signalling into bone and muscle.
AG: Intermediate receptor activity.
AA: The longer, less active receptor. Sunlight and vitamin D status carry more weight for you — measure it, and let a real number rather than a genotype decide anything.

markers.impact: Vitamin D receptor (TaqI) — receptor expression in bone and muscle

AA: The common expression pattern. Ordinary vitamin D advice applies.
AG: Intermediate expression.
GG: Associated with different receptor expression; effects are population-dependent and small. Reported, not acted on alone.

markers.impact: The protein that carries vitamin D around your bloodstream

AA: Efficient vitamin D transport — you carry more of what you make or eat.
AC: Intermediate transport. Sensible sun exposure most days does most of the work.
CC: Lower carrier protein, so circulating vitamin D reads lower for the same sunlight. One of the best-replicated markers here. The action is a blood test, not a bottle — and if it is genuinely low, sunlight first.

markers.impact: The second carrier-protein variant — binding affinity for vitamin D

AA: Higher binding affinity. Total vitamin D reads higher; free vitamin D is what actually acts.
CC: Lower binding affinity — total vitamin D can read lower while free vitamin D is fine. Worth knowing before anyone treats a number rather than a person.

markers.impact: Activates vitamin D in the liver — the first conversion step

AA: Efficient first activation step.
AG: Intermediate activation.
GG: Slower first activation. Combined with the carrier results above, this is an argument for measuring rather than assuming.

markers.impact: The core clock gene — sets whether your body leans early or late

AA: The earlier-leaning setting. Mornings genuinely are easier for you, and your best work is likely to happen before lunch.
AG: Slightly later lean. Your natural window is mid-morning to early evening — protect the first hour of the day rather than fighting it.
GG: The later-leaning setting, replicated across several cohorts. You are not undisciplined; your clock runs later. Bright light within thirty minutes of waking and dim light after sunset shifts it earlier by real minutes — this is the highest-return habit in your whole report.

markers.impact: Clock gene linked to morning preference and to how stress shifts your timing

GG: The common setting. Your clock holds its position under ordinary pressure.
AG: Associated with morning preference. Your timing is fairly robust to a late night, but not to a late week.
AA: Less common. Associated with morning preference and with a clock that shifts more when stress is high — regular meal and light timing steadies it.

markers.impact: Links the clock to blood-sugar handling overnight

AA: Common setting. Overnight glucose regulation tracks your last meal more than your clock.
AC: Intermediate. Late heavy eating shows up in your morning readings more than in most people's.
CC: Associated with different overnight glucose handling. Finishing your last real meal three hours before bed is the practical version of this result.

markers.impact: Clock partner gene tied to sleep timing and duration

GG: The common setting; sleep timing sits where you put it.
AG: Intermediate; small association with shorter sleep duration.
AA: Associated with slightly shorter natural sleep and later timing. Anchor the wake time and let the bedtime find itself.

markers.impact: The melatonin receptor sitting on your insulin-producing cells

CC: Melatonin and blood-sugar control stay out of each other's way.
CG: Carrier. Eating late — while melatonin is already up — handles blood sugar less well for you than the same meal earlier. One of the best-replicated findings in nutrition genetics.
GG: Both copies. Late-night eating is measurably worse for you than for most people, independent of what you eat. Finish eating before melatonin rises and this simply resolves. High leverage, one habit.

markers.impact: The final enzyme that makes melatonin

AA: Standard melatonin production.
AG: Intermediate. Evening light discipline matters more than any supplement here.
GG: Associated with lower melatonin output. Darkness after sunset is the actual intervention — melatonin production responds to light far more than to genotype.

markers.impact: The receptor caffeine blocks — decides whether coffee sharpens you or rattles you

TT: The sensitive setting. Caffeine reliably produces anxiety, a racing pulse and a wrecked night for you at doses other people call normal. This is not low tolerance; it is a different receptor. Halve the dose and stop by early morning, and caffeine becomes useful again.
CT: Intermediate sensitivity. Caffeine works well early and costs you sleep if it drifts past midday.
CC: Low sensitivity at this receptor. Caffeine is a mild, usable tool for you rather than a lever.

markers.impact: The liver enzyme that clears caffeine — a fourfold difference between people

AA: Fast caffeine clearance. Coffee clears quickly for you, and a mid-afternoon cup is unlikely to reach your sleep. Timing is the useful part here; nothing about quantity follows from a genotype.
AC: Intermediate clearance. Caffeine still works, but the tail is longer than you think — a 15:00 coffee is still in you at 23:00. Move your cut-off to noon and see what your sleep does.
CC: Slow clearance. Caffeine stays in your system for many hours, and in slow metabolisers the performance benefit largely disappears while the sleep cost remains. Morning only, and a real cut-off. This single change usually outperforms every supplement someone has ever sold you.

markers.impact: Adrenaline receptor variant linked to naturally short, efficient sleep

GG: The common setting. Your sleep need is ordinary and real.
CG: Carrier. Associated in one well-studied family with shorter natural sleep. Check it against measured nights before you trust it.
CC: Associated with shorter natural sleep. SAM will believe your device before it believes this marker.

markers.impact: The strongest known marker for restless legs and periodic limb movement in sleep

TT: Low likelihood of restless-legs-type disruption.
GT: Carrier. If your legs feel restless in the evening or your sleep looks fragmented without you remembering waking, ask for a ferritin — low iron stores are the commonest treatable driver, and it is a simple test.
GG: Both copies of the associated variant at the best-replicated restless-legs locus. Worth a ferritin test and a conversation with your doctor if evenings are uncomfortable or your nights look fragmented on the band. Very treatable.

markers.impact: Second restless-legs marker — also linked to iron handling in the brain

CC: Low likelihood on this marker.
CT: Carrier. Combined with the marker above, worth watching evening leg comfort and checking ferritin once.
TT: Both copies. Same practical step: a ferritin test, and treat the cause rather than the symptom.

markers.impact: A GABA receptor subunit tied to sleep spindles and to how alcohol affects your night

CC: Standard GABA signalling through sleep.
CT: Intermediate. Alcohol's effect on your deep sleep is likely to be noticeable on the band even when you feel fine.
TT: Associated with altered GABA signalling and stronger sensitivity to alcohol's effect on sleep architecture. The measurable version: two drinks costs you more deep sleep than it costs most people. Look at your own data for a week and decide from that.

markers.impact: Serotonin receptor involved in slow-wave sleep and emotional processing

GG: Standard receptor density. Emotional processing overnight runs quietly.
AG: Intermediate. Sleep quality and mood are more tightly coupled for you than average — a bad night shows in your temper before it shows in your legs.
AA: Associated with altered receptor density. Same practical point: protect REM, especially the second half of the night, which is where alcohol and late caffeine do their damage.

markers.impact: The rate-limiting enzyme for serotonin in the brain

GG: Standard serotonin synthesis capacity.
GT: Intermediate. Daylight, movement and protein-containing meals feed this pathway more reliably than anything in a bottle.
TT: Lower synthesis capacity in some studies. Practical levers with real evidence: outdoor light in the morning, aerobic exercise most days, and adequate protein. This is the pathway that most rewards ordinary living.

markers.impact: The autoreceptor that decides how much serotonin gets released

CC: Standard autoreceptor function — the brake sits where it should.
CG: Intermediate. Associated with a slightly stronger stress-linked mood response.
GG: More autoreceptor expression, less serotonin release. Associated with stronger emotional reactivity under load. Sleep and social contact move this more than most people expect.

markers.impact: Breaks down serotonin, dopamine and noradrenaline. On the X chromosome, so men carry one copy

CC: Higher turnover of monoamines. Mood shifts resolve quickly.
CT: Intermediate turnover.
TT: Lower turnover — monoamine signals last longer, for better and worse.
C: One copy (X-linked). Higher turnover; mood shifts pass quickly.
T: One copy (X-linked). Lower turnover, so both good and difficult moods have a longer tail. Note: SAM does not use the 'warrior gene' framing. That came from one small study, it did not replicate, and it has done real harm.

markers.impact: A calcium channel gene consistently linked to mood regulation

GG: The common setting.
AG: Carrier. Associated with slightly stronger emotional reactivity — sleep regularity is the strongest countermeasure.
AA: Both copies. Same point, more so: your mood is measurably more sensitive to sleep timing than to almost anything else you could change.

markers.impact: The oxytocin receptor — social connection, empathy and how much other people steady you

GG: Associated with stronger responsiveness to social support. Time with people you like is a genuine physiological recovery tool for you.
AG: Intermediate. Social recovery works; it just is not the whole answer.
AA: Associated with drawing less regulation from social contact and more from solitude and structure. Neither is better — knowing which one recharges you is the useful part.

markers.impact: How quickly your cortisol response switches off once the stressor has passed

CC: Efficient cortisol shut-off. You come back down quickly after a spike — a real advantage under sustained pressure.
CT: Intermediate. The shut-off works; it is slower if sleep is short. Protect the wind-down hour.
TT: Slower cortisol shut-off, replicated across many cohorts. Stress lingers physiologically after it has ended psychologically — which is why you can feel fine and still sleep badly. A genuine wind-down routine, consistent sleep timing and morning light are the highest-return habits in your report.

markers.impact: Clears dopamine and adrenaline from the thinking part of the brain. The single most useful marker in this report

AA: Met/Met — slow clearance. Dopamine lingers in the prefrontal cortex, which gives you excellent sustained focus and working memory in calm conditions, and a sharp drop-off when pressure spikes. Practically: prepare hard, then protect calm before the moment that matters. Your caffeine tolerance under stress is lower than you think. This is the classic mental-athlete profile — brilliant when the room is quiet.
AG: Val/Met — the balanced setting. You hold focus in calm conditions and under pressure. The most common and most forgiving result at this locus.
GG: Val/Val — fast clearance. You need stimulation to reach your best thinking: deadlines, competition and noise genuinely help you, and quiet low-stakes work is where you drift. Build urgency into the work rather than waiting for it. Under real pressure you are at your sharpest, which is a rare thing.

markers.impact: The growth factor behind learning, memory and recovery from stress

GG: Standard BDNF release. Skill learning and memory consolidation run efficiently.
AG: Carrier. Slightly less activity-dependent release — which makes the things that raise BDNF matter more, not less: aerobic exercise, sleep and genuinely new learning.
AA: Both copies. Aerobic exercise is the strongest known way to raise BDNF in humans, and for you it is doing more work than it does for others. Consistent movement is a cognitive intervention here, not a fitness one.

markers.impact: Taq1A — a proxy for how many dopamine D2 receptors you have. Note: this variant sits in ANKK1, not DRD2

GG: Standard D2 receptor density. Reward feels proportionate to effort, and habits form on the ordinary schedule.
AG: Carrier. Somewhat lower receptor density — you may need a bigger signal to feel the same reward. Make progress visible, because a number you can see does real work for you.
AA: Lower receptor density. Effort can feel less rewarding in the moment, which makes structure beat motivation every time: scheduled sessions, visible progress, a training partner. Nothing here is about willpower — it is about how loudly the reward arrives.

markers.impact: Receptor availability in the striatum — the drive-and-habit circuit

CC: Higher striatal receptor availability. Habits stick well once started.
CT: Intermediate availability.
TT: Different receptor distribution, associated with more prefrontal and less striatal dopamine signalling. Practically: you are better at deliberate planning than at automatic habit — so use calendars rather than relying on routine to form itself.

markers.impact: Converts dopamine into noradrenaline — the balance between drive and alertness

GG: Both copies. Same direction, more so. Regular aerobic movement is the lever that answers this one.

markers.impact: Acetylation speed — a second route for clearing caffeine's breakdown products, and many other compounds

TT: Fast acetylation on this allele. Caffeine by-products and other amines clear briskly.
CT: Intermediate. Read together with the second NAT2 marker and with CYP1A2 — acetylator status needs both.
CC: Slow acetylation on this allele. Combined with slow CYP1A2 it lengthens how long caffeine's downstream products hang around.

markers.impact: The second acetylation variant — the two together define fast or slow acetylator status

GG: Fast acetylation on this allele.
AG: Intermediate. Acetylator status is a two-marker call, not a one-marker one.
AA: Slow acetylation on this allele. Slow acetylators clear a range of compounds more gradually — worth knowing, and not a reason to change anything on its own.
